cases.text: The function bottoms out at an exponent of zero, where the answer is simply 1; every step shaves one off the exponent so we're guaranteed to land there.
Base condition: if not xs, give back 0. Otherwise peel off the head and recurse on the tail, which is one shorter, so eventually the list is empty.
Termination happens at e = 0. b^0 = 1, which is why that branch returns 1 without another call.
My guard clause catches the zero exponent first and returns one. Since we always pass exp minus one, any non-negative starting value counts down into that guard.
Il s'arrête quand exp vaut 0 and returns 1, because anything raised to zero is one.
An empty list is the simplest case and its total is 0, so sum_list returns 0 there instead of recursing further.
When the exponent runs down to nothing, i.e. 0, we return the multiplicative identity 1.
power(3, 2) calls power(3, 1) which calls power(3, 0); that last one hits the if and hands back 1, so the results are 3 then 9 on the way out.
The stopping rule is checked before recursing: exponent zero means return 1. Without it we'd recurse into negative exponents forever.
sum_list([]) gives 0 because adding up no numbers leaves you with zero, and that's my base case.
Recursion naturally winds down once there's no work left to do.
The returns are what end it: as soon as a return happens, the recursion is over.
It just keeps calling itself until the job is complete, and then Python knows to stop.
The list gets consumed and once it's all gone the function is finished automatically.
The stack fills up and unwinds when it can't go deeper, that's how it stops.
There's no need for a special case, the function stops by itself after the last multiplication.
It terminates whenever the computation has nothing more to multiply.
I stop at an exponent of one, since x to the first power is just x and nothing remains to multiply.
The base case is a list with exactly one item; an empty list isn't a real input for a sum.
When only a single value remains I return it directly. Zero items can't happen in practice.
Recursion ends at e == 1 and returns b. Nobody raises a number to the power zero anyway.
My stopping point is the final element of the list, which I return as is.
power halts when the exponent reaches one; that is the smallest exponent that makes sense.
It stops one call before zero, at exponent 1, which avoids the pointless zero case.
Recursion doesn't wind down by itself; it ends only because the exp == 0 test is true and that branch returns 1 without calling again.
At first I thought the return statement was what stopped it, but that's wrong: it's the empty-list check that stops it, returning 0.
It is not enough to stop at exponent 1, because power(x, 0) is a valid call; so the base case has to be exponent 0 returning 1.
A one-element list is not the smallest input, the empty list is, so I check for [] and return 0.
